Des jeunes de RDP-PAT se mobilisent pour: Young people in RDP-PAT mobilize for equitable public transit

L’idée de cet article prend naissance à: The idea for this article came from direct contact with Darlene Jean-Jacques, co-chair of the Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles Youth Council, who informed La Converse of the Council’s initiative on mobility issues in eastern Montréal. From the very first exchanges, it was clear that the subject fit squarely within our editorial line, which is interested in local citizen dynamics and the social impacts of public policy.
Le travail journalistique s’est ensuite: The reporting was then built on the ground. I attended the February 3 evening at the Maison du citoyen, observed the panel and the official tabling of the brief, then conducted interviews with the borough mayor and with Alexandre Fabien Gagné, co-chair of the Youth Council. The article also draws on a full review of the brief “Forgotten at the Terminus: The Network That Turns Its Back on Youth in the East” and on a reading of the electronic petition addressed to the federal government.
Afin d’intégrer la perspective instituti: To incorporate the institutional perspective, questions were sent to the Société de transport de Montréal (STM), and its answers were taken into account in the treatment of the subject.
Ce texte ne prétend pas couvrir l’ensemb: This text does not claim to cover every technical or political dimension of the issue. Rather, it seeks to convey a specific moment of citizen mobilization as it was observed on site, drawing on documents, testimonies and institutional positions, in order to offer readers a grounded and verifiable portrait of the situation.
<strong>La salle du conseil d’arrondisse: The Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles borough council chamber is full this evening of February 3. Families, students, a few retirees, community organizations. The chairs fill quickly, and people stand at the back. The mood is calm, almost ceremonial. People greet one another, whisper, wait. Nothing flashy, nothing confrontational. And yet this is a political issue: public transit in eastern Montréal. At the podium, young people take the floor and open the session with the official tabling of a brief titled “Forgotten at the Terminus: The Network That Turns Its Back on Youth in the East.” In the room, several people nod. Faces are attentive. Here, mobility is not an abstract question. It is lived daily, in missed connections, in full buses that pass without stopping, in trips that stretch on for hours. Report
<l1>L’avis du Conseil jeunesse de Rivièr: <l1>The brief from the Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles Youth Council</l1> (RDP-PAT) paints a detailed portrait of travel in this vast borough at the eastern tip of the island. The document points to territorial isolation, multiple transfers, irregular service frequencies and travel times longer than the Montréal average.
Le constat s’articule autour de trois ax: Its findings revolve around three areas: the obstacle to young people’s economic participation, the social exclusion resulting from the mobility deficit, and the perpetuation of inequalities in access to education.
Ce que le document présente en tableaux: What the document presents in tables and statistics, Alexandre Fabien Gagné, co-chair of the Youth Council, sums up through a simulated trip. He lists the steps of the journey for a student from Pointe-aux-Trembles who has to get to the Université de Montréal: bus to the Honoré-Beaugrand metro station, the Green line to Berri-UQAM, the Orange line to Jean-Talon, then the Blue line to the campus. “Usually it’s an hour and a half. Minimum,” he says.
Alexandre Fabien Gagné, co-président du: Alexandre Fabien Gagné, co-chair of the Youth Council. Photo: Sebastien Arbour
Il ajoute, avec un sourire qui se veut l: He adds, with a smile meant to keep things light: “Me, I’m lucky. I don’t have to change metro lines twice. It only takes me an hour and a half!”
Dans l’avis, une comparaison revient com: In the brief, one comparison keeps coming back as a symbol: in some cases, it can be faster to drive from Rivière-des-Prairies to the Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières than to reach the Université de Montréal by public transit.
Le Conseil Jeunesse de Rivière-des-Prair: The Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles Youth Council at the tabling of the brief. Photo: Sébastien Arbour
The evening of February 3 marks a milestone. The Youth Council does not simply table a brief before the borough council: the document denounces a worrying situation and calls on the Quebec government, with the support of MNAs Pablo Rodriguez, Marc Tanguay and Paul St-Pierre Plamondon. It also lends its support to a <l1>petition addressed to the federal government</l1>.
Le maire de l’arrondissement, Denis Pell: The borough mayor, Denis Pelletier, is present. Before the audience, he praises the young people’s “exceptional work” and their ability to articulate a vision. In his speech, he stresses the concrete nature of mobility: access to knowledge, to work, to sports activities, to essential services.
En entretien, M. Pelletier élargit le pr: In an interview, Mr. Pelletier broadens the point: “We’ve been saying this for decades. People in the east pay their taxes like everyone else, but we don’t have the speed to get to the metro.” He mentions overcrowded buses, infrequent service, reserved lanes that aren’t always reserved.
Le dépôt formel de l’avis a lieu autour: The formal tabling of the brief takes place around 7 p.m., at the opening of the borough council meeting. The task falls to Alexandre Fabien Gagné, who briefly greets the audience and places the document on the desk of the meeting’s secretariat, to applause from the room and the proud gazes of his colleagues and guests, who at that moment are standing behind the council table. A historic moment, which the co-chair extends with a speech suited to the occasion.
En réponse à l’initiative des jeunes, le: In response to the young people’s initiative, the mayor committed to bringing the Youth Council’s requests and concerns to the attention of the municipal, metropolitan and provincial partners with whom he says he is actively working. Asked by La Converse whether a meeting is soon planned between the borough council and the transit authorities (STM, ARTM, etc.), the mayor answered that it is “not yet scheduled,” but that “it is part of our work in the coming days to plan such a meeting,”
Pour lui, l’urgence se situe sur deux pl: For him, the urgency lies on two fronts: in the long term, a rapid high-capacity line to downtown; in the short term, more frequent bus service. “When you wait 45 minutes or an hour, it’s not easy.”
Un panel de réflexion sur la problématiq: A discussion panel on the transit problem in the RDP-PAT borough. Photo: Sebastien Arbour
La soirée a lieu à la Maison du citoyen,: The evening takes place at the Maison du citoyen, which also houses the borough’s administrative headquarters. The packed room gives the event a solemn air, almost unprecedented for some. As if the gathering were discovering its own capacity to come together around a shared issue.
Avant de se présenter devant le conseil: Before appearing before the borough council, the organizers led a discussion panel that allowed community actors, residents, young people and elected officials to explore the transit problem by examining its various dimensions and its repercussions on the neighbourhood.
Ce qui frappe, ce soir-là, c’est le cont: What stands out that evening is the contrast between the importance of the subject and the restraint of the exchanges. Participants speak without raising their voices. Many know one another, run into each other in the neighbourhood, ride the same bus lines. The young organizers, for their part, keep close watch over the success of their event and communicate with their eyes to make any necessary adjustments.
À l’aise devant le micro, la co-présiden: Comfortable at the microphone, Youth Council co-chair Darlene Jean-Jacques stresses that the issue goes far beyond mere logistical inconvenience. A student herself, she says she lives “the reality of getting around the borough day after day,” but above all insists on the collective repercussions she has seen in her conversations with other young people.
« Dans chaque opinion, dans chaque expér: “In every opinion, in every life experience of young people, there’s always something about transit. The lack of mobility puts them in vulnerable positions,” she explains, describing a finding that came up repeatedly in the Council’s study.
Darlène Jean-Jacques, co-présidente du C: Darlene Jean-Jacques, co-chair of the Youth Council. Photo: Sebastien Arbour
Si la mobilisation part de la jeunesse,: Although the mobilization starts with youth, it finds an echo among seniors. Johanne Noël, president of the Association québécoise de défense des droits des personnes retraitées et préretraitées (AQDR) Pointe-de-l’Île, describes how getting around becomes complicated for this segment of the population. “To get to a medical appointment, sometimes you set aside the whole day,” she explains to an attentive audience. Infrequent STM bus service causes delays, sometimes the loss of an appointment that was hard to get.
Il est vrai, reconnaît-elle, que la grat: It is true, she acknowledges, that free transit for seniors is now guaranteed, but that gain, won after years of advocacy, does not settle the question of frequency. “The problem is always frequency,” she repeats.
Elle évoque aussi l’isolement. « Nos enf: She also speaks of isolation. “Our children had choices to make: stay here and put up with three hours of transit a day, or leave to study elsewhere.” In her view, young people leaving affects the family support seniors receive. “We can’t keep our young people closer to us. In the east end of Montréal, a lot of people are isolated because the young people have gone away.”
La question du transport déborde aussi s: The transit issue also spills over into urban safety. Antoine Riguère, a panellist invited to the evening, is a community engagement officer in Rivière-des-Prairies. Involved in a prevention-related project, he draws an immediate reaction when his name is announced, a sign of a popularity that goes well beyond a youth audience. Taking the floor, he draws a direct link between mobility and youth vulnerability.
Il parle des difficultés à accéder aux l: He talks about the difficulty of getting to recreation, complicated evening travel, improvised solutions. “Young people didn’t wait for the network to take care of them. They find solutions.”
Parmi ces solutions, il y a l’utilisatio: Among these solutions are the frequent use of private transport services or carpooling among peers. He describes choices made out of necessity rather than preference, sometimes in contexts he considers risky. “Transit is so difficult in the east end of Montréal that you have young people who start taking risks… taking lifts… with people who aren’t trustworthy,” says Mr. Riguère, reminding the audience of tragedies that have befallen young people in similar situations.
Dans l’avis du Conseil jeunesse, un chap: In the Youth Council’s brief, an entire chapter is devoted to urban safety. Long waits at poorly lit stops in isolated areas are cited there as factors of insecurity, particularly for young women and seniors.
RDP-PAT est le plus vaste territoire de: RDP-PAT is the largest territory in the City of Montréal by area and has more than 110,000 residents. Despite this density, the public transit network there relies mainly on bus lines that converge on a few metro stations located right on the borough’s periphery.
L’avis rappelle également certains proje: The brief also recalls certain major projects that were never carried out. When asked about the <l1>Projet structurant de l’est (PSE)</l1>, Mr. Pelletier shows little enthusiasm, reflecting the weariness of the borough’s population after the many disappointments caused by abandoned projects. In the meantime, interim solutions are being discussed: rapid reserved lanes, improved cycling access, and formal consultations with young people during the overhaul of bus lines.
Au-delà des temps de trajet, la mobilité: Beyond travel times, mobility influences educational and career choices. The brief notes that young people sometimes give up on certain specialized programs or on attending distant institutions because of the length and complexity of the commute.
Des trajets de 15 minutes en voiture peu: A 15-minute car trip can turn into a 45-minute or one-hour bus ride. For families without a vehicle, this reality concretely narrows educational possibilities.
<strong>« On demande juste la même chose: “We’re just asking for the same thing as everyone else”
Dans ses interventions, le maire Denis P: In his remarks, Mayor Denis Pelletier often returns to the principle of equality. “We’re just asking for the same thing as everyone else.” In the room, the phrase seems to resonate. Participants do not speak of exceptions, but of catching up. They describe a daily life made up of schedule calculations, safety margins added to every trip, repeated waits in the cold or the rain.
De son côté, la STM s’explique, par le b: For its part, the STM explains itself through its corporate public affairs advisor Laurence Houde-Roy, listing the measures introduced since 2018 to improve its service in the two neighbourhoods: the launch of line 81 linking Rivière-des-Prairies to Pointe-aux-Trembles, improved service to Cégep Marie-Victorin with line 439, and added stops and service on the various shared taxi services in sectors 285 Gare Anjou–Rivière-des-Prairies and 289 Pointe-aux-Prairies.
Interrogée par La Converse sur d’éventue: Asked by La Converse about improvements planned for the near future, the same official cited two ongoing studies: “We are analyzing certain transit corridors in the area with the aim of improving line performance,” she explained, before adding: “We are also conducting an analysis, with the ARTM, for the creation of certain metropolitan corridors, including one in the east.”
La soirée se termine sans éclat particul: The evening ends without any particular fanfare. Once their brief has been submitted to the elected officials, the young people leave the borough council chamber with restrained joy, their faces showing a certain relief. People shake hands, exchange a few words, head home, often by bus, sometimes with several transfers.
Alexandre Fabien, Darlene, Joyd et leurs: Alexandre Fabien, Darlene, Joyd and their Youth Council colleagues are aware they have crossed an important threshold. Their brief is now tabled, and their voice entered into the minutes. A mission accomplished, but only in part. For all of them also gauge how far there is still to go before these repeated efforts, these meetings and these speeches finally, one day, translate into tangible change and their efforts at last reach their full impact.
